Payal put the cup down, opened her email, and started typing to Ramesh sir.

passage: My first job, at twenty-three, was checking loan forms at a bank's back office in Indore. I was fast. By two o'clock my pile was done, and then I'd drift: news, cricket scores, a long walk to the water cooler. I felt guilty all the time, like a fraud with an ID card. I asked for more forms. More forms didn't help. It was the same form, only more. What changed things was small. Eshaan, from the branch, took me along one day to meet a woman who ran a tailoring shop. She showed me the two machines the loan had paid for. I saw the form I'd checked, turned into her shop. After that the forms felt like people. I still got restless, but less. I think my boredom wasn't asking for more work. It was asking for a reason. Devika, still learning what boredom asks for.

qa.a: The two machines the loan had paid for.

Supervisor's note, lab team, Friday

Over the past two weeks I've noticed a change in Sangeeta, one of our most careful technicians. Her samples are done by noon. Then she wanders: long phone breaks, reorganising the reagent shelf twice, chatting at the door. When I asked yesterday, she apologised at once and said she felt guilty for "wasting the afternoon."

I first assumed she was under-challenged and offered her the new testing protocol. She looked more tired at the idea, not excited. When we talked longer, she mentioned she had covered night shifts for three weeks while a colleague was on leave. I don't think this is a need for harder work. I think it's exhaustion showing up as restlessness.

Next step: I've taken her off the night rota for two weeks. We'll revisit the new protocol after that.

— Francis

Ujjwal used to put up his hand in maths. This term, he has stopped. Today, when I gave the fractions sheet, he wrote "whatever" at the top and put his head down. When I asked why, he said, "I get it wrong anyway. Even when I try, sir, you say it's wrong." I realised he has had three red-pen sheets in a row, and he was also scolded at home for his marks.

I sat with him and gave him one sum only, halves of a chapati, drawn on the board. He got it right. He looked at me as if he didn't believe it. I gave him a second. Right again. I'll start each class this week with one sum I'm sure he can do.

A Monday in July. Sarita's desk lamp flickered and died. She didn't mention it. She studied by the ceiling light, squinting. Her cousin Ishita, staying with them for the summer, noticed. "Tell Chacha. He'll get a new one." Sarita shrugged. "It's fine."

The next Sunday. The lamp still dead. Ishita watched Sarita's eyes water over her chemistry notes. "Why don't you ask?" Sarita looked at the floor. "When I was small, I asked for things. Nobody listened. Now I just don't." "But Chacha isn't like that anymore. You've seen him." Sarita said nothing.

A Friday, two weeks later. With Ishita beside her, Sarita stood at the kitchen door and said, quickly, "Papa, my lamp is broken." Her father looked up. "Since when? Why didn't you say?" That evening he came home with a new lamp. Sarita held it a long time before switching it on.

passage: Afreen, you're new to teaching, so let me tell you about Manoj. Twenty years ago, my first batch at the polytechnic. Manoj was bright, I could see it in his questions. But every assignment, he'd write one line and hand it back. "Sir, I can't do drawings. I always fail." I felt angry at first, honestly. Then I felt sad. passage: Samir, you ask why I always say, speak to someone early? Let me tell you about my twenty-fifth year. I worked in the accounts office of a textile mill in Surat. The ceiling leaked onto my desk. I asked the manager to fix it. Nothing. I asked for a proper chair for my back. Nothing. After a year, I stopped asking. I just moved my files when it rained. I stopped feeling angry, even. I felt nothing. I'd come home, sit, stare at the wall. My sister Rukhsana noticed. She said, "Rafiq bhaijaan, you're not tired, you're gone." She took me to a counsellor at the community clinic. I felt embarrassed at first. But talking helped me see I had stopped trying everywhere, not just at work. Slowly, with help, I started looking for another job. Two years later I left.

passage: The monsoon had started, and the ceiling of Nilesh's rented room in Thane was dripping into a bucket again. He had messaged the landlord four times since April. His friend Damini came over with a tarpaulin and saw him sitting on the bed, just staring at the bucket. "Nilesh, when did you last go out?" He couldn't remember. She sat down. "This isn't just the leak. Will you talk to someone? The college has a counsellor." He hesitated, then nodded. That evening, with Damini beside him, he booked an appointment for the next day.

passage: In the Bandra office, Hafsa had asked her manager three times for training on the new software. Three times it was "next quarter." She had also asked to move off the night shift. Silence. By October she had stopped asking anything. In meetings she nodded. At lunch she ate alone. When Sunaina from the next desk mentioned a team outing, Hafsa said, "What's the point?" without looking up. Sunaina noticed that Hafsa's plants on the desk had dried out, the ones she used to water every morning. One evening she stayed back. "Hafsa, you seem really far away lately. Can I help?" Hafsa shrugged, then her eyes filled. "I don't feel anything anymore." Sunaina didn't try to fix it. She said, "The company has a free counselling line. Want to call now? I'll sit with you." Hafsa hesitated, then picked up the phone.

passage: When I was ten, my toy car's wheel came off. I wanted to give it to Papa to fix, like always. But my cousin Preeti said, "Try it yourself first." I was annoyed. I thought I'd break it more. passage:
A Monday in September. Eshaan's parents had begun living apart, and he sat in the school counsellor's room, unable to sit still. "Everything is falling apart and I can't stop it." Nirmala ma'am handed him a sheet with two columns. "Let's sort it. What can you control, and what can't you?"

That Wednesday. He brought the sheet back. Can't control: whether they fight, where Papa lives, the money stuff. Can control: my study hours, calling Nani on Sundays, telling Nirmala ma'am when it's bad, going to football. He looked at it for a long time. "The first list is bigger." "But the second list is yours," she said.

Three weeks later, a Friday. Eshaan had studied every evening from six to eight, called Nani twice, and played football on Saturdays. At home things were still hard. But he walked into the counsellor's room without dragging his feet. "I feel less... helpless," he said.

qa.q: What did Eshaan write under 'can control'?
qa.a: His study hours, calling Nani on Sundays, telling Nirmala ma'am when it's bad, and going to football.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when he said 'The first list is bigger'?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and a bit hopeless, seeing how much of the situation was out of his hands.

qa.q: Which choice helped Eshaan, and why?
qa.a: Acting on the 'can control' list, such as study hours and calling Nani, gave him real proof of what he could do, which eased his sense of helplessness.

qa.q: How might Nirmala ma'am see Eshaan's change after three weeks?
qa.a: She would likely be pleased to see him steadier, even though the home situation is still hard.

grounding: It shows a teenager facing his parents' separation who lists what he can and cannot control, and feels less helpless by acting on the first list over several weeks.

passage: Ujjwal, you're worried about your father's job. Let me tell you what I did, at your age. When I was fifteen in Ludhiana, my father's cloth shop closed. He sat home all day, silent. Ma cried in the kitchen. I felt like the ground had gone. I couldn't study, couldn't sleep. One night, I tore a page from my notebook and made two lists. Things I can't change: the shop, Papa's mood, the loans. Things I can: my board exam study, helping Ma with the cooking, talking to my science teacher, playing hockey. I pinned it above my bed. Every day I did one thing from the second list. It didn't fix the shop. But I stopped feeling like a leaf in the wind. That's what Baljeet learned at fifteen, puttar.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a teenager in a hard family situation, listing what was and wasn't in their control and acting on the first list restored some power for Baljeet.

passage: Nilesh's grandmother was in the hospital in Nashik, his parents were there every evening, and his board exams were three weeks away. At home there was one phone, which his mother took to the hospital. He felt pulled in every direction. His friend Vaibhav came over with chai. "You look like a lost cow." Nilesh laughed weakly. Vaibhav pulled out a notebook. "Two lists. What can you do something about?" Nilesh thought. "Study two hours every morning before school. Keep the house clean so Ma doesn't worry. Ask Sir for past papers." "And what can't you?" "Aaji getting better. The hospital bills. Papa's mood." He stared at the second list, then turned the page back to the first. The next morning he was at his desk at six. When his mother came home that night, the dishes were washed.
